en.title: Stick Season 2: Owen Wilson's Coaching Comeback Delivers Deeper Drama
en.summary: Apple TV+'s beloved sports comedy "Stick" returns for its second season, delving deeper into the personal struggles of its titular coach. Owen Wilson leads an ensemble cast in a season promising more heart and emotional resonance.
en.body:
The whistle has blown, and **Apple TV+**'s **"Stick"** is back on the field for its highly anticipated second season. Picking up where the first left off, this season promises to build upon the foundation of heartfelt sports drama and endearing character work that made its debut so compelling. At its core, **"Stick"** follows the journey of **Pryce** (played with signature charm by **Owen Wilson**), a man grappling with his past while trying to guide a team toward success. Like its spiritual predecessor **"Ted Lasso"**, the series masterfully blends the therapeutic power of sport with the messy, beautiful complexities of found family and personal healing.

Season 2 is set to explore **Pryce**'s unresolved history even further, moving beyond the breezy underdog story into more profound territory. **Owen Wilson** delivers one of the finest performances of his career, embodying a 55-year-old man-child facing a critical crossroads. His portrayal captures the poignant struggle of seizing a last chance at opportunity before the specter of regret looms too large. The series doesn't shy away from the paternal baggage and past traumas that shape its characters, weaving them into an inspirational narrative that feels both earned and deeply moving. The ensemble cast, including **Marc Maron** as the cynically protective **Mitts**, continues to provide essential support, acting as the Sancho Panza to **Pryce**'s Don Quixote.

## A Deeper Dive into the Roster

The sophomore season isn't just about **Pryce**; it expands the narrative to encompass the entire team and their individual arcs. The introduction of **Rhea Seehorn** in a supporting role is a welcome addition, promising to add another layer of nuanced performance to the already strong ensemble. Returning favorites like **Peter Dager**, **Mariana Treviño**, **Lilli Kay**, **Judy Greer**, and **Timothy Olyphant** are expected to further flesh out their characters' stories, making the surrogate family dynamic even richer. The series creators have emphasized their commitment to delivering a heartfelt and feel-good experience, and Season 2 appears poised to deliver on that promise with even more emotional depth and resonant storytelling.

## What the Fans Can Expect

For the dedicated fanbase of **"Stick"**, Season 2 represents a significant upgrade and a deepening of the emotional stakes. The series has already cultivated a loyal following drawn to its unique blend of humor, sports drama, and authentic human connection. The promise of exploring the characters' pasts and continuing their journeys of redemption and self-discovery is exactly what fans have been hoping for. The show’s ability to balance inspirational comeback stories with genuine emotional struggles, all while featuring top-tier musical choices, has cemented its place as a must-watch on **Apple TV+**. The growing complexity and the expanded focus on the supporting cast ensure that the emotional investment fans have in this surrogate family will only grow stronger.

## What's Next

The second season of **"Stick"** officially premieres on **November 4, 2026**, with two episodes, followed by weekly installments until December 30, 2026. Viewers can anticipate a continuation of the emotional journey that has captivated audiences, with more character development and heartwarming moments on the horizon.

content_raw: It’s impossible to ignore the similarities between the Apple TV series “ Ted Lasso ” and “ Stick ,” as both follow the therapeutic sports-comedy playbook. These shows feature tremendously likable actors in the lead role as deeply broken coaches who use the purity and poetry of a sport to build an endearing surrogate family while trying not to unravel from past trauma and paternal baggage. Both series feature amicable divorces, viral meltdowns, tested loyalties, inspirational comeback stories and top-tier needle drops—and both pull off an impressive balancing act that compels us to follow the journeys of not only the leads, but more than a half-dozen supporting players. We could go on, but we’ll stop after this note: Whereas Jason Sudeikis’ Ted would almost be lost without Brendan Hunt’s wonderfully eccentric and fiercely loyal Coach Beard, Owen Wilson ’s Pryce has Marc Maron ’s equally protective but infinitely more cynical Mitts. Both Don Quixotes have their Sanchos Panza. “Stick” isn’t in quite the same instant-classic league as the Emmy award-winning, pop culture-dominating “Ted Lasso,” but Season 2 is a remarkable upgrade from the already engaging first season. Yes, Owen Wilson is doing his familiar laid-back, soft-rebel-with-a-heart-of-gold thing, but he’s tailor-made for the role. As the second season delves even further into Wilson’s Pryce “The Stick” Cahill’s unresolved past, the series proves to be more than a breezy underdog sports comedy/drama. Wilson does some of the finest work of his career as a 55-year-old man-child, given perhaps his last real chance to embrace opportunity before he’s relegated to a lawn chair on a driving range in Fort Wayne, forever lamenting what might have been. (And who he could have wound up with.) As Pryce puts it, in a crossroads moment: “Maybe it’s better to go through life believing you could have been great than to find out you couldn’t.” But what a waste of a life that would be. Season 2 finds Pryce with some measure of purpose, thanks to his mentorship of Peter Dager’s Santi Wheeler, a troubled teenager turned sensational golf prodigy who, at 18, is wavering between taking a full ride to Indiana University and turning pro. John Higgins (from the “Please Don’t Destroy” comedy sketch group) joins the cast as the oily, relentless sports agent Jeremy Pierce, who dazzles Santi with splashy Hollywood parties and promises major endorsements if he joins Jeremy’s high-end agency. Higgins is just the start of this season’s expanded cast. Billy Zane is in prime, slick, unctuous form as Jeremy’s boss. Rhea Seehorn , fresh off her Emmy win for “ Pluribus ,” adds great spark as Amanda Lydecker, who has known Pryce since they were teenagers and is the daughter of Pryce’s first coach and mentor, Butch Lydecker (Rex Linn), who is living with dementia. (This is a reunion for Seehorn and Linn; on “ Better Call Saul ,” Seehorn played Kim Wexler, while Linn played Kevin Wachtell, CEO of Mesa Verde Bank and Trust.) W
